reason: The objective is a comparison of revenue directions at a fixed price change, and the misconception in the case is definitional, not dynamic: elasticity is the ratio of percentage changes, epsilon = (dQ/dP)(P/Q), which varies along a single straight demand curve while its slope stays constant. An animated price slider hides the 'before' price-quantity rectangle at exactly the moment the comparison has to be made, and watching a point crawl along one line actively encourages reading steepness as elasticity. Two labelled snapshots plus a total-revenue plot keep all four revenue numbers and the epsilon values visible at the same time, which is where the direction difference actually lives.
staticAlternative: One static figure with two linked panels. Panel A: the single linear demand Q = 100 - 5P (P from 0 to 20) with three marked points and their elasticities and revenues, P = 2 (Q = 90, epsilon = -0.11, revenue 180), P = 10 (Q = 50, epsilon = -1.0, revenue 500), P = 18 (Q = 10, epsilon = -9.0, revenue 180); the slope is the same at all three, so the student sees that elasticity is not slope. Panel B: the total-revenue hump TR = P(100 - 5P) on the same P axis, peaking at P = 10. Two arrows on the hump show the same one-unit price rise: P 2 to 3 raises revenue 180 to 255 (inelastic region) while P 18 to 19 lowers it 180 to 95 (elastic region). A caption states the rule: with inelastic demand a price rise raises revenue, with elastic demand it lowers revenue, and the revenue test therefore reads elasticity off the direction of change rather than off the steepness of the line.
